title: CSS Fundamentals: Selectors, Cascade, and the Box Model
description: Learn how CSS rules match elements, how the cascade decides between conflicting declarations, how stylesheets are attached, and how the box model and display values affect layout.
learningOutcomes: Choose between external, internal, and inline CSS and explain their trade-offs.
Read basic type, class, and ID selectors.
Predict which declaration wins when rules conflict under the same cascade conditions.
Explain content, padding, border, and margin and apply border-box sizing.
Distinguish block, inline, and inline-block behavior while building a small landing page.

blocks.text: HTML describes the structure and meaning of content; CSS describes how that content should look and be laid out. Keeping these roles separate makes it easier to change a design without rewriting the document, reuse the same visual rules across pages, and inspect problems systematically. A CSS declaration is a property/value pair, such as color: rebeccapurple. A rule combines a selector—which chooses elements—with a declaration block containing one or more declarations.

blocks.title: Read a CSS rule from the outside in
blocks.text: First ask which elements the selector matches. Then inspect the declarations that apply to those elements. If several declarations target the same property, the cascade resolves the conflict; source order is only one part of that decision, not a universal “last rule always wins” rule.

items: External stylesheet: keep rules in a .css file and attach it with a link element in head. This is usually the best default for a real multi-page application because the same file can style many pages and responsibilities remain separated.

Internal stylesheet: put rules inside a style element in the document head. This can be useful for a self-contained demonstration or a page-specific experiment, but shared styles become harder to maintain if copied across pages.

Inline style: write a declaration in an element's style attribute. It is useful in limited cases where a value is generated for a particular element, but it couples presentation to markup and is awkward to reuse. It also participates in the cascade differently from ordinary selector rules.

blocks.caption: Attach an external stylesheet from the document head
blocks.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Study Notes</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="./styles.css">
</head>

blocks.text: Selectors: choose the elements a rule targets

A type selector matches elements by tag name, a class selector begins with a dot and matches the class attribute, and an ID selector begins with # and matches an id value. Classes are usually the most reusable choice for styling components. IDs should identify a unique element in a document and generally should not be the everyday tool for reusable styling.

blocks.caption: Type, class, ID, and descendant selectors

blocks.text: When multiple declarations could set the same property on one element, the browser uses the CSS cascade to decide which one applies. The complete algorithm considers origin and importance, cascade layers, specificity, scoping proximity where relevant, and then source order. For beginner-level debugging, when declarations have the same origin, importance, layer, and scope conditions, compare selector specificity; if specificity is also equal, the later declaration wins.

steps.title: The reusable class rule
steps.explanation: The class selector matches every element with class=card__title. Its specificity is one class component.

steps.title: The more specific rule
steps.explanation: This selector combines an ID selector and a class selector. Under the same cascade origin, importance, layer, and scoping conditions, its specificity is higher, so the title inside the element with id=featured-card becomes purple.

steps.title: Why not just move the rule later?
steps.explanation: Moving the lower-specificity rule later would not make it beat the higher-specificity rule under these conditions. Do not add increasingly specific selectors or !important as a first response; inspect which declaration wins and choose the simplest maintainable rule.

blocks.title: Specificity is not the whole cascade
blocks.text: This lesson compares ordinary author rules under the same cascade conditions. Important declarations, cascade layers, user/browser styles, and scoping can affect the result before source order is considered. When DevTools disagrees with a simple specificity calculation, inspect the full cascade rather than assuming the browser is wrong.
The box model: content, padding, border, and margin

A CSS element is laid out as a box. The content area holds text or other content. Padding is the space between the content and the border. The border surrounds the padding and content. Margin creates space outside the border, separating the box from neighboring boxes. These areas solve different layout problems; using margin to create space inside a card, for example, is not equivalent to using padding.

steps.title: Use border-box sizing consistently
steps.explanation: With box-sizing:border-box, the declared width and height include the content, padding, and border. Applying this rule to pseudo-elements too helps keep sizing predictable.

steps.title: Declared width versus inner content
steps.explanation: The card's total border-box width is 320px. Because padding and the 2px borders are included in that width, the content area is narrower than 320px. With the default content-box model, the same declared width would describe only the content and the rendered outer width would grow by padding and borders.

steps.title: Margin is outside the border
steps.explanation: The block-axis margin adds external separation between cards; it does not increase the declared border-box width. Horizontal and vertical margins may interact with surrounding layout rules, so inspect the rendered box in DevTools.

steps.title: The selector can affect a nested title
steps.explanation: The class sets a reusable default title color. The ID-plus-class selector overrides it for the featured card under the cascade conditions explained above.

items: block: normally starts on a new line and participates in block layout; width and height can be applied.
inline: flows inside a line of text. Width and height do not behave like they do for block boxes, and vertical margins do not separate lines in the same way.
inline-block: flows inline with surrounding content but accepts width and height like a block-level box.
Changing display changes layout behavior, not the semantic meaning of the HTML element. Do not pick a semantic element only because its default display looks convenient.

blocks.prompt: With box-sizing: border-box, a block has width: 320px, padding: 16px on each side, and a 2px border on each side. What is the total border-box width?

options.feedback: Border-box includes content, horizontal padding, and both borders within the declared 320px width.
Adding padding and borders to 320px would describe the total with content-box, not border-box.
This incorrectly adds extra space beyond the declared width; border-box already includes padding and border.
This subtracts the padding from the total but omits the border; 288px would not be the total border-box width.

blocks.explanation: The declared border-box width already includes the content, 32px of horizontal padding, and 4px of horizontal border; the content area shrinks to fit.

blocks.prompt: If two CSS declarations have the same origin, importance, layer, specificity, and scoping conditions, the later declaration wins when both set the same property on the same element.

options.feedback: When the earlier cascade criteria are equal, source order is the tie-breaker and the later declaration wins.
Source order does resolve the conflict after the stated higher-priority cascade conditions and specificity are equal.

blocks.explanation: Source order is the final tie-breaker in this simplified case, not a rule that overrides higher specificity or other cascade criteria.

blocks.prompt: Which statements about CSS authoring methods are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An external stylesheet can be shared by several HTML pages
options.feedback: A linked CSS file can be reused so design changes do not require copying declarations into every page.

options.text: A style element inside head is an internal stylesheet
options.feedback: Rules inside a style element are part of the document's internal stylesheet.

options.text: A style attribute on an element is inline CSS
options.feedback: The style attribute attaches declarations directly to one element's markup.

options.text: Inline CSS automatically creates a reusable design system for multiple pages
options.feedback: Inline declarations are attached to individual elements; they do not automatically provide reusable shared styling.

blocks.explanation: Each method can be understood by where the declarations live and how easily they can be reused and maintained.

blocks.title: Build a small landing page and style its boxes
blocks.context: Create a simple landing page with a header, main content, two cards, and a footer. Use CSS to establish typography, spacing, borders, and display behavior. The editor supports an isolated HTML preview; it does not run JavaScript.
instructions: Use a complete HTML document and include a style element in head so you can preview the result in this exercise.
Add a header, a main region with a page heading, two content cards, and a footer.
Create a reusable .card class and a .card__title class.
Apply box-sizing: border-box consistently and explain what the card's width includes.
Use padding for space inside each card, border to outline each card, and margin to separate cards.
Give the second card id=featured-card and style its heading using a more-specific selector.
Try block, inline, or inline-block on a small element and describe the visible difference.
After the exercise, move the CSS into styles.css and attach it with a link element.
requirements: The HTML has a clear heading hierarchy and semantic header, main, and footer regions.
The two cards share reusable class-based styles.
The stylesheet contains type, class, and ID selectors.
The featured title's color difference can be explained using the cascade and specificity.
The box model is intentional: padding is internal, margin is external, and border-box sizing is used.
The page displays without horizontal overflow at a 320px viewport.

successCriteria: The landing page uses one clear page heading and semantic page regions.
Both cards receive the same reusable class styles.
The featured title receives a different color because its selector is more specific under the shown conditions.
The card width remains predictable with border-box sizing.
You can explain the difference between content, padding, border, and margin.
You can describe one practical difference between block, inline, and inline-block.

items: Selectors determine which elements match a rule; declarations set property/value pairs.
External CSS is usually the maintainable default for shared application styles; internal and inline CSS have narrower uses.
The cascade considers more than source order. Compare specificity only after higher-priority cascade criteria are understood.
The box model comprises content, padding, border, and margin. Border-box sizing includes padding and border in the declared width.
Block, inline, and inline-block affect layout behavior but do not change an element's semantic meaning.
